description: Reverse any text character by character, flip the order of words, or mirror each word in place. Everything runs instantly in your browser with no uploads.

faq.a: Whole text flips every character end to end, word order reverses the sequence of words while keeping each word intact, and each word mirrors every word individually.
faq.q: What is the difference between the three modes?

faq.a: Yes — reversal is done per Unicode character, so emojis, Urdu script and other non-Latin text stay intact.
faq.q: Does it handle emojis and Urdu text correctly?

faq.a: No. Reversal happens entirely in your browser; nothing is uploaded or stored.
faq.q: Is my text sent anywhere?

howTo: Paste your text into the input box.
Pick a mode: whole text, word order, or each word.
Copy the reversed result with one click.
name: Text Reverser
tagline: Flip text, words or word order

description: Collapse multiple spaces into one, trim every line, and drop empty lines from pasted text. Perfect for cleaning up copied content before publishing or pasting into forms.

faq.a: No — single spaces between words are kept. Only runs of two or more spaces or tabs are collapsed into one.
faq.q: Will it remove single spaces between words?

faq.a: Yes. The trim and remove-empty-lines options are applied to every line separately.
faq.q: Does it work on multi-line text?

faq.a: Yes — pasted PDF text with scattered extra spaces is exactly what this tool is for.
faq.q: Can I clean text with weird spacing from PDFs?

howTo: Paste the messy text into the input box.
Tick the cleanup options you want: collapse spaces, trim lines, remove empty lines.
Click Clean Up and copy the tidy result.
name: Remove Extra Spaces

description: Arrange lines alphabetically, by number, or by length with one click, or shuffle them randomly. Ideal for tidying lists, names, and data rows.

faq.a: Lines are sorted by their leading number; lines without a number are placed at the end in alphabetical order.
faq.q: How does numeric sorting handle lines without numbers?

faq.a: Blank lines are removed by default; untick 'Remove blank lines' to keep them in the sort.
faq.q: What happens to blank lines?

faq.a: Yes — it uses the browser's cryptographic random source with a Fisher–Yates shuffle, so every order is equally likely.
faq.q: Is the shuffle truly random?

howTo: Paste your list, one item per line.
Choose a sort mode: A–Z, Z–A, numeric, or by length.
Copy the sorted list — or hit Shuffle for a random order.
name: Sort Lines
tagline: Sort lines A–Z, numerically or shuffle

description: Prefix every line with a number in the style you choose — 1., 1), [1] or #1 — starting from any number. Great for referencing list items in documents and code reviews.

faq.a: Yes — enter any starting number and the sequence continues upward from there.
faq.q: Can I start numbering from a number other than 1?

faq.a: Yes, every line gets a number, including blank ones, so the numbering always matches the original line count.
faq.q: Are blank lines numbered too?

faq.a: Four styles: 1. with a dot, 1) with a parenthesis, [1] with brackets, and #1 with a hash.
faq.q: Which formats are available?

howTo: Paste your text, one item per line.
Pick a number format and the starting number.
Copy the numbered list.
name: Number Lines
tagline: Add line numbers in your format

description: Scan pasted text and pull out every email address automatically, with optional duplicate removal. Useful for building contact lists from documents and pages.

faq.a: Yes — the scanner reads the whole text and picks out anything shaped like an email address, wherever it appears.
faq.q: Does it find emails inside long paragraphs?

faq.a: By default, yes — duplicates are matched case-insensitively so the list is clean.
faq.q: Are duplicates removed?

faq.a: Completely. Extraction runs locally in your browser and nothing leaves your device.
faq.q: Is the text I paste private?

howTo: Paste the text containing email addresses.
Keep 'Remove duplicates' ticked to get unique addresses.
Click Extract Emails and copy the clean list.
iconSvg: <rect x="3" y="5" width="18" height="14" rx="2"/><path d="M3 7l9 6 9-6"/>
name: Extract Emails
tagline: Pull email addresses from any text

description: Find every web link hidden in a block of text, from full https addresses to plain www domains. Optionally remove duplicates and copy the clean list.

faq.a: Yes — plain www.example.com style links are detected too, not just full http(s) addresses.
faq.q: Does it detect links without https://?

faq.a: Yes. Trailing commas, periods and closing brackets that are not part of the URL are trimmed automatically.
faq.q: Does it strip trailing punctuation from links?

faq.a: Yes — it works on any pasted text, including chat logs, emails and documents.
faq.q: Can I use it on chat or email exports?

howTo: Paste the text containing links.
Keep 'Remove duplicates' ticked to get unique URLs.
Click Extract URLs and copy the list.
name: Extract URLs
tagline: Pull links out of any text

description: Paste HTML markup and get back clean, readable plain text with all tags removed. The tool also reports how many tags were stripped.

faq.a: Your browser parses the markup with its built-in HTML parser and reads out only the visible text, so even broken or nested tags are handled safely.
faq.q: How are the tags removed?

faq.a: Their contents are not treated as visible text, so script and style code does not pollute the output.
faq.q: What happens to scripts and styles?

faq.a: No — everything is processed locally in your browser.
faq.q: Is my HTML uploaded anywhere?

howTo: Paste your HTML markup into the input box.
Click Strip HTML Tags.
Copy the plain text — the tool shows how many tags were removed.
name: Strip HTML

description: Paste two versions of a text to see exactly what changed: added, removed and modified lines are highlighted for easy review. Handy for checking edits to drafts, lists and code.

faq.a: Green lines were added in B, red lines were removed from A, and amber lines were changed between the two versions.
faq.q: What do the colours mean?

faq.a: It compares line by line. A line that differs in any character is shown as changed, with the old and new versions shown together.
faq.q: Does it compare word by word?

faq.a: Very large texts are rejected with a warning to keep the comparison fast — typical documents and code files work fine.
faq.q: Is there a size limit?

howTo: Paste the original text into box A.
Paste the new version into box B.
Click Compare Texts and review the highlighted differences.
name: Text Diff
tagline: Compare two texts line by line

description: Count how often each character or word appears and see the results ranked with visual bars. A quick way to analyse writing patterns or check for overused words.

faq.a: The top 100 most frequent characters or words are listed, ranked from most to least common.
faq.q: How many items are shown?

faq.a: Untick 'Ignore case' to treat A and a (or The and the) as different items.
faq.q: Can I count uppercase and lowercase separately?

faq.a: When whitespace counting is on, ␣ marks a space, ⇥ a tab and ↵ a line break.
faq.q: What do the special symbols mean?

howTo: Paste your text into the input box.
Switch between Characters and Words modes.
Review the ranked table with counts and percentages.
name: Character Frequency

description: Translate English into playful Pig Latin and decode Pig Latin back to English. The reverse translation is a best-effort guess, since Pig Latin is ambiguous.

faq.a: Words starting with a vowel get 'way' added; other words move their leading consonant cluster to the end and add 'ay' — so 'hello' becomes 'ellohay'.
faq.q: How does the translation work?

faq.a: Pig Latin is ambiguous: 'ayway' could decode to 'way' or 'ay'. The tool picks the most likely word, but unusual words may decode imperfectly.
faq.q: Why is decoding marked best-effort?

faq.a: Yes — capitalisation of the first letter and surrounding punctuation are preserved in both directions.
faq.q: Are capital letters and punctuation kept?

howTo: Choose the translation direction.
Type or paste your text.
Copy the translated result.
iconSvg: <circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8"/><circle cx="9.5" cy="12" r="1.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><circle cx="14.5" cy="12" r="1.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/>
name: Pig Latin Translator

description: Turn any sentence into the classic mocking SpongeBob meme format with randomised capitalisation. Every click produces a fresh random mix.

faq.a: Yes — the Re-roll button generates a brand new random capitalisation of your sentence every time.
faq.q: Can I get a different random mix of the same text?

faq.a: No. Only letters are randomised; numbers, spaces and punctuation stay exactly as typed.
faq.q: Are numbers and punctuation affected?

faq.a: It mimics the mocking SpongeBob meme, where alternating random capitals suggest a sarcastic, imitating tone.
faq.q: What is this meme format?

howTo: Type your sentence into the box.
Click RaNdOmIzE to randomise the capitalisation.
Copy it — or hit Re-roll for a different mix.
name: SpongeBob Case

description: Delete all whitespace, just line breaks, just tabs, or collapse everything into single spaces. Also trims the start and end of every line on demand.

faq.a: All whitespace deletes every space, tab and line break; collapse replaces each run of whitespace with a single space, keeping the text readable on one line.
faq.q: What is the difference between 'All whitespace' and 'Collapse to single spaces'?

faq.a: Yes — after running, the tool reports exactly how many whitespace characters were removed.
faq.q: Does it show how much was removed?

faq.a: Yes — choose 'Trim each line' to remove leading and trailing spaces on every line while keeping the line structure.
faq.q: Can I trim each line without deleting the line breaks?

howTo: Paste your text into the input box.
Choose what to remove: all whitespace, line breaks, tabs, or more.
Click Remove and copy the cleaned text.
name: Whitespace Remover
tagline: Strip spaces, tabs and line breaks

description: Restyle plain text into bold, italic, script, monospace, circled or upside-down Unicode lettering. Copy any style straight into bios, captions and usernames.

faq.a: They use special Unicode letters rather than formatting, so they display anywhere that supports Unicode text — no app feature needed.
faq.q: Why do these styles work on Instagram and WhatsApp?

faq.a: Letters and digits convert; symbols and punctuation that have no styled equivalent are left unchanged.
faq.q: Will every character convert?

faq.a: Often poorly — the styled letters have odd Unicode names, so avoid fancy text for important accessibility content.
faq.q: Can screen readers read fancy text?

howTo: Type your text into the input box.
Preview all six styles instantly.
Copy the style you like into your bio or post.
name: Fancy Text
